source: ACIAR AH/2005/086 'Smallholder Cattle Best Practice Manual' (Windsor, Bush & Young), Best Practice Health and Husbandry of Cattle, Cambodia -- hosted at mekonglivestock.wordpress.com (University of Sydney / GDAHP project site)
text: Breeding in Cambodia is often unmanaged, from free-roaming animals with no bull selection; the manual recommends instead using selected, higher-quality bulls (often via a fee-for-service arrangement). Healthy, non-pregnant mature females should cycle into heat every 21 days, though the signs (restlessness, bellowing, mounting behaviour, mucous vaginal discharge) may only show for a few hours and are easy to miss, especially in buffalo or in tethered animals unable to display normal herd behaviour -- the key sign to watch for is the cow standing to be mounted. Gestation is roughly 9 months, with two-thirds of foetal growth happening in the last 3 months, so the cow needs 2-2.5 times maintenance-level energy through late gestation and lactation; underfeeding at this stage delays her return to heat, often until the calf is weaned, reducing lifetime calf output. Using a pregnant or lactating cow for draught work is therefore not recommended. Male calves not being kept as breeding bulls should generally be castrated by an experienced operator with proper aftercare to prevent infection. Calves are especially vulnerable to the roundworm parasite Toxocara vitulorum -- poor-doing calves should have faecal samples checked, and anthelmintic treatment within the first 3 weeks of life manages the infestation. Calves over 6 months, like adults, can also be affected by the liver fluke Fasciola gigantica; few common anthelmintics treat liver fluke, so veterinary help is advised.
